I am a former heroin addict with just over a decade clean. Medication assisted therapy saved my life. I began seeing an addiction psychiatrist and began buprenorphine maintenance in November of 2015, a few months before people started dropping like flies from fentanyl. 

In the years since, I have gone back to school, built a career in healthcare, gotten engaged, and have built a life that I can finally feel proud of. 

That said, some things never truly recovered. My relationships with my friends, whose trust I shattered, have never recovered. At best, we exchange cordial text messages once or twice a year, but I am not invited to birthdays, weddings, or even casual evenings at pub trivia. I spend most of my free time either alone or with my fiancé. It's hard to build new friendships in your mid 30s, and the loneliness is the hardest part.

 I am never going back to the days where I was controlled by addiction, and I am proud of everything I have built since I entered treatment, but I am still haunted by the idea that I broke some things that can never be truly repaired.

Having lived through addiction, I was deeply moved by the story of Sergei Kochegarov. I empathize with him deeply, and hearing that his daughter was happy to see him had me fully in tears. Stay strong, Sergei. Your life is worth it. 

To anyone struggling with addiction, life CAN get better. It is not easy, and you will need help (which I hope you can access), but life can get better.

comments.body: Migraine is a complex neurological disease that may well have a genetic component. Vestibular migraine is one form the disease may take. Abdominal migraine (pain, nausea, vomiting, digestive conditions often initially misdiagnosed as IBS  but without headache) is another form, but there are ocular forms, and others. Abdominal migraine is more common in children, but adults also suffer from it. Changes in sinus pressure (watery nose and eyes may be affected) and misdiagnosed as "allergies" are also possible, as are experiencing strange smells, being hypersensitive to noise ("jumpiness," /quick to startle), smelling things that aren't there, episodes of tinnitus, oversensitivity to even light touch and noise. The nervous system seems primed for sudden over-reaction--and "auras" may include anxiety and depression just before episodes. Some researchers consider migraine a form of epilepsy, involving the brain more directly, while others focus on hormonal causes, or ways to calm the nervous system down--whether through medication, meditation, exercises, quiet solitude, or other means. Migraine is poorly understood as a systemic, whole-body, condition, and it often runs in families. People of all ages can develop it, and it may disappear in one form (headaches) only to appear later in life in another. People with migraine are too often dismissed as chronic complainers or hypochondriacs, but those who have experienced any form of migraine need careful, whole body evaluation.

All good for Tallamy and his 10 acres in a presumably rural or exurban setting, but here, in my suburban NY community, I am surrounded by homeowners who depend on lawn care companies to care for their properties, which means heavily fertilized lawns drenched in weed killers, blasted weekly by leaf blowers, and gardens containing  a small and repeating assortment of anodyne and limited plant species. 

Yes, I agree with Tallomy on the benefits of planting a wide variety of natives, but the issue that goes deeper is the lack of emotional connection to the land, and thus the abandonment of responsibility toward the land. I'm 73, and when I was young, hardly anyone in my then neigborhood of private homes hired lawn care companies; they are now ubiquitous. My garden is mostly all native, and rich in species, and I don't use weedkiller nor blower, but a 75 by 100 foot lot set within a landscape of poisoned, manicured, leaf debris-free lawns, is not enough by itself to sustain the multiplicity of plant and insect species needed for a healthy ecosystem. I don't think I've seen a praying mantis in over 20 years, and this year, I have seen only one Monarch Butterfly, though I have a thriving population of milkweed, and hardly any ladybugs.
Suburbanites  have been told by Scotts et al., that they should want a lawn to be green and neat, and that if they can afford it, let strangers care for their property. Alienation from the natural world is a different problem, but it is relevant.

comments.name: 77Stillworking
comments.body: I make a living negotiating difficult legal cases.  On occasion, I have asked ChatGPT what move it thinks I should make in the next round of negotiations.  90 percent of the time I disagree with ChatGPT's suggestion.  When I ask ChatGPT what a reasonable outcome of the negotiation should be, I have yet to resolve a negotiation in the manner recommended by ChatGPT.  What ChatGPT does not understand is the way people think and more importantly the way people feel.  Negotiating disputes is driven as much by what a lawyer had for breakfast that morning as any bundle of rational arguments supporting the lawyer's position.  I recently heard two "tech savvy" non-lawyer opine that future courtroom cases will largely be conducted by AI proof and persuasion.  Nothing could be further from the "truth".  Anyone who has any experience in trial (and I have spent hundreds of days in the courtroom) knows the outcome of trials is largely unpredictable and juries often surprise us with their verdicts.  Intuition, life experiences, and personal morality have as much to do with trial verdicts as any precise rhetorical examination of the evidence.  In my opinion, AI will never be able to successfully compete fully  with the complexity of the human spirit and imagination. Our humanity is not defined by X's and O's.  We have evolved over millions of years because we are dream-weavers as much as we are rationalistic tacticians.  When we surrender our dreams to machines, we will lose our capacity to wonder, to explore, and to hope.

The current state of the AAA game industry is a tale of the pitfalls of modern managerial corporatism. The notion is that when you have money, you buy up successful franchises to secure even more market share and produce a reliable source of revenue. Microsoft owns virtually every title that made the AAA game market what it is today through its acquisitions of Activision Blizzard (Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, Overwatch, Diablo, StarCraft), ZeniMax Media / Bethesda (The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, Doom, Wolfenstein, Quake), and smaller single title acquisitions (Minecraft, Halo, Gears of War, Age of Empires, Fable).

It then proceeded to either ruin them via committee, wind them down, or shutter them entirely. Despite having billions of dollars pumped into them the Halo franchise is puffing along on fumes thanks to successive and remarkably strange creative decisions. Call of Duty has become a bogged down nightmare. The Elder Scrolls won't have another title until 2028 (likely 2029) representing an almost 20 year gap between titles. Fallout has been flailing around with its ill conceived MMO and doesn't have another title even planned until the 2030s.

Microsoft is like the Disney of the gaming world. It keeps buying geese that lay golden eggs, forcing the geese to go through intensive rounds of brand optimization, and getting confused when all it gets are lumpy chunks of lead and dead geese.

Here in the United States, according to the USDA, 9 Billion chickens are killed each year with 48.9 billion pounds of meat expected for 2026. I feed them well including treats of sunflower seeds from my garden and dandelions from my yard, greens that a grocery store gives me for free because they're the outer leaves of romaine and cabbage.  On really hot days like today, I give them a small treat of watermelon which they greatly appreciate. Every month I clean out their coop and add it to my compost pile which eventually enriches my garden.

I share the extra eggs with neighbors and friends and they are always amazed at how good they taste in comparison to what they buy in the store.  

I try to spend a few minutes each day just observing them. Placidly clucking and scratching the ground. Same as it ever was. It's a daily moment of Zen.

If you've got the space, you could do worse than keep a few backyard chickens. Even with these increased heat waves. In my opinion, backyard chickens are one answer to what is ailing us as people: disconnection from the source of our food, disconnection from other species, disconnection from our shared earth.

Trump seems to think that a $77 billion monthly deficit means that we sent $77 billion in cash to other countries in exchange for nothing.  That's wrong.  When we send $77 billion to other countries, other countries send us MORE than $77 billion worth of goods.  Why do I say "MORE than"?  Because that's how free trade works.  When I buy a pencil from you for a dollar, it's because I want the pencil MORE than the dollar and you want the dollar MORE than the pencil.  When we exchange one for the other, it's still the same dollar and it's still the same pencil.  But somehow both of us feel wealthier.  That's the magic by which capitalism CREATES wealth by bringing together people with different needs and values.  Anyway...it works the same way with the trade deficit.  Americans buy foreign products because we want the products more than we want the money it costs to buy them.  So no matter how much money we send overseas, we get back MORE value in products (and services).  There's only a trade deficit because we buy more from other countries than they buy from us.  But who cares?  We're still wealthier as individuals and as a nation than if we didn't buy the things we want/need from them.

The carbon cycle for the last 2 million years was doing 180-280ppm atmospheric CO2 over 10,000 years and we’ve done more change than that in 100 years. The speed of change now is much greater than virtually anything we have found in Earth’s climate history.

The last time CO2 went from 180-280ppm global temperature increased by around 4 degrees C and sea level rose 130 meters. (See graph below, 1) It takes time for temperature and sea level to equilibrate with elevated atmospheric CO2 and we could blow much further off of that graph.

One amplifying feedback alone out of dozens, loss of albedo or heat reflectivity from Arctic summer sea ice melt, over the last several decades has been equivalent to 25 percent of the climate forcing of anthropogenic CO2. And that will continue to increase as that ice largely disappears by mid century.

The Titanic sank because by the time the lookout called the warning the ship had too much momentum to turn. The Earth has a lot more momentum, e.g. we've already likely locked in at least 6 meters of sea level rise from the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and decade to decade warming in the near term is also virtually locked in.

That momentum is building and the higher we let global temperatures rise the greater the risk of them going really high as amplifying feedbacks strengthen.

1.  (graph of the last 400,000 years of global temperature, CO2 and sea level https://www.ces.fau.edu/nasa/images/impacts/slr-co2-temp-400000yrs.jpg )

The most important line on Earth, the shoreline, is moving inland. A foot of sea level rise doesn’t sound like much, but a rise in sea level of 1 foot, averaged globally, moves the shoreline inland 300 feet, and it's worse in places like S Florida and Bangladesh.

One foot of sea level rise on the US NE coast caused hurricane Sandy to flood an additional 25 square miles.

One problem with sea level rise is the closer sea level approaches the top of a coastal defense the greater the risk of storm surge breaching the defense as in New Orleans with hurricane Katrina.

As a result many of our large coastal cities and seaports will not go away slowly with sea level rise but quickly in catastrophic storms.

articles.title: Want more babies? We need more friends.
articles.summary: If Americans are to revive our sagging national birthrate, we must rebuild ordinary social structures.

comments.name: Procladius
comments.body: Good luck, but I suspect that the birth decline is irreversible. There are too many negatives associated with having more than one or two children. That's really not such a bad thing, since space and resources are finite, and no society can support an ever - growing population. We will have to cope with a declining population that will eventually stabilize at a lower level than today.
